candidate.scope: Single-molecule droplet barcoding (SMDB), restricted to the assigned Illumina SMDB schematic row: DNA templates are encapsulated, amplified, fragmented, barcoded and pooled for library preparation. The neighbouring Drop-ChIP/scChIP-seq, partial scATAC-seq and BS-Seq/Bisulfite-seq/WGBS rows and right-side chemical legend are context outside this target. The left SMDB icon and expansion label identify the assay rather than another transformation. No alternative target workflow or analysis operation is drawn.

features: Reagent interface resolved from the primary paper; not separately drawn as a branch in the poster.

features: DNA fragments carry droplet-specific barcode sequences.
Shared barcodes retain the association between fragments and their original template.
Droplet compartments are still drawn at this boundary.
Primary-source clarification: barcodes are attached through adaptor homology, rather than being a label on the droplet wall.
A droplet-specific barcode is an intended template association; co-encapsulation and droplet coalescence can produce mixed associations.

evidence.quote: Templates are fragmented inside drops, and barcodes are attached to fragments such that each droplet gets a unique barcode sequence.

After the templates have been fragmented, the barcodes used to tag fragments belonging to the same template are attached by overlap-extension PCR in the droplets (Fig. 2c). In this reaction, barcode sequences attach to the fragments through regions of sequence homology on the adaptor sequences added by the transposase.
Instances of multiple templates in the same barcode cluster are infrequent, and consistent with the rate of co-encapsulation expected by Poisson statistics (see Supplementary Note 3 for details).

Even with the small size, ∼10–50% of droplets coalesce (Supplementary Fig. 3a), which is undesirable since it can lead to multiple templates or barcodes in a single droplet, and hence improper barcoding.

states.label: Pooled barcoded DNA for sequencing
features: Final blue DNA fragments have short coloured tags; individual droplets are no longer drawn.
Sequenced material represents fragmented copies of input DNA templates, with barcodes preserving template association.
Barcode-grouped short reads can support reconstruction of template sequence and detection of template variants; these data-analysis steps are not drawn as operations in the assigned row.
Primary-source clarification: droplet rupture releases DNA contents, so this endpoint is pooled DNA rather than a collection of intact droplets.
Template identity and sequence recovery are not guaranteed to be perfect: the primary paper reports mixed-template barcode groups and uneven sequence coverage.

evidence.quote: All fragments are sequenced in parallel and resulting reads are clustered based on barcode. Clustered reads are used to reconstruct the sequence or accurately detect SNPs for the template encapsulated in each droplet.
The remaining droplets are chemically ruptured and the DNA contents are purified over a spin column, then size selected to remove free barcodes, resulting in a sequence-ready library.
Instances of multiple templates in the same barcode cluster are infrequent, and consistent with the rate of co-encapsulation expected by Poisson statistics (see Supplementary Note 3 for details).
However, bias in sequencing can yield excessive coverage in certain regions and insufficient coverage in others.

operations.label: Single template encapsulation
operations.description: Partition input DNA templates into separate droplets, producing isolated single-template compartments and empty droplets.
operations.mechanism: Droplet microfluidic encapsulation; the primary figure states that most droplets contain zero or one template.
operations.information_effect: Physical compartmentalization establishes the unit whose fragments will later share a barcode.

operations.label: Template amplification
operations.description: Copy each isolated template to produce a clonal DNA population within its droplet. The output contains multiple copies rather than the single input molecule.
operations.mechanism: In-droplet clonal amplification; amplification chemistry is unspecified in the poster.

operations.label: Template fragmentation
operations.description: Convert amplified template copies into shorter DNA pieces while retaining separate template compartments. The poster shows fragmentation; the primary paper clarifies that Tn5 also adds adaptor sequences needed for the following barcode attachment.
operations.mechanism: Tn5 transposase fragments amplified DNA and attaches adaptor sequences within droplets; it acts as a reagent in this operation.
operations.information_effect: Sequence information is distributed among shorter pieces while the droplet preserves their common template origin.

evidence.quote: Templates are fragmented inside drops, and barcodes are attached to fragments such that each droplet gets a unique barcode sequence.
To fragment in the droplets, we use a microfluidic device to add Tn5 transposase into each droplet, which randomly fragments and attaches short sequences to the amplified templates25 (Fig. 2b).
The transposase reaction inside droplets fragments templates while adding adaptors to each fragment.
Importantly, fragmentation must be performed while maintaining compartmentalization, to prevent pieces of different templates from mixing before barcodes have been attached.

operations.label: Barcode every droplet
operations.description: Attach droplet-specific DNA barcode sequences to the adaptor-bearing fragments produced by the preceding fragmentation block. The output DNA physically carries a template-origin tag. The diagram also retains an empty-droplet icon, so its caption is not evidence that every compartment yields template-derived library DNA.
operations.mechanism: Primary-source resolution: barcode droplets are merged with fragmented-template droplets and PCR reagent; overlap-extension PCR joins barcodes to fragments through homology on the transposase-added adaptors. This is one local barcoding operation in the assigned schematic.
operations.information_effect: Barcode sequences carried on the DNA fragments preserve the association of pieces from an input molecule after pooling. This supports grouping short reads by template; co-encapsulation and droplet coalescence can compromise that association.

evidence.quote: Templates are fragmented inside drops, and barcodes are attached to fragments such that each droplet gets a unique barcode sequence.
DNA barcodes uniquely tag all reads derived from a template, which allows the reads to be unambiguously clustered to generate a long and accurate consensus sequence for the template.

After the templates have been fragmented, the barcodes used to tag fragments belonging to the same template are attached by overlap-extension PCR in the droplets (Fig. 2c). In this reaction, barcode sequences attach to the fragments through regions of sequence homology on the adaptor sequences added by the transposase.
This step thus requires merging three droplets: template, barcode and PCR reagent.
Uniquely barcoding millions of DNA templates requires tens of millions of ‘barcode droplets', each containing a clonal population of one barcode sequence.
Instances of multiple templates in the same barcode cluster are infrequent, and consistent with the rate of co-encapsulation expected by Poisson statistics (see Supplementary Note 3 for details).

Even with the small size, ∼10–50% of droplets coalesce (Supplementary Fig. 3a), which is undesirable since it can lead to multiple templates or barcodes in a single droplet, and hence improper barcoding.

operations.label: Pool for library prep
operations.description: Pool barcoded DNA for library preparation, yielding the tagged DNA endpoint shown without droplets. The primary paper resolves this boundary as chemical rupture of the emulsion and recovery of DNA contents. The poster presents library preparation as a broad block.
operations.mechanism: Chemical rupture removes droplet boundaries and permits DNA contents to be recovered together; the recovered barcoded fragments form the sequence-ready library after preparation.
operations.information_effect: The pooled DNA contains fragments of amplified original templates. Physically attached barcodes permit short reads to be grouped for template consensus reconstruction, SNP detection and within-template variant linkage. These are supported readout uses, not additional operations drawn in this row; uneven coverage and mixed barcode groups limit recovery and assignment.

method_scopes.rationale: SMDB is the sole assigned target. The poster expands its name as single-molecule droplet barcoding, and the verified catalogue heading and primary paper identify the same isolate/amplify/fragment/barcode architecture. All five operations belong to this route. The amplification block is generic; the primary Figure 2 reports PCR or MDA implementations, which are components rather than additional target methods. The separate barcode-reagent state records a primary-supported input interface to the depicted barcoding block, not another depicted workflow. Adaptors, barcode attachment chemistry and droplet rupture are primary-supported clarifications of the poster blocks. Neither purification details nor barcode-reagent manufacture is expanded into extra operations. The source reports non-ideal template assignment and coverage, so a shared barcode supports molecule-level inference without guaranteeing it. Repeated droplet icons represent a population of separate compartments on one route, rather than separately named alternative workflows or a pool before barcoding.

evidence.quote: Lan F et al. (2016) Nat Commun 7:11784
In this paper, we describe single-molecule droplet barcoding (SMDB), an ultrahigh-throughput method to barcode long molecules for short-read sequencing.
DNA templates are encapsulated into droplets such that most droplets contain zero or one template.
Templates are clonally amplified to produce multiple copies in each droplet.
Templates are fragmented inside drops, and barcodes are attached to fragments such that each droplet gets a unique barcode sequence.

All fragments are sequenced in parallel and resulting reads are clustered based on barcode. Clustered reads are used to reconstruct the sequence or accurately detect SNPs for the template encapsulated in each droplet.
To fragment in the droplets, we use a microfluidic device to add Tn5 transposase into each droplet, which randomly fragments and attaches short sequences to the amplified templates25 (Fig. 2b).

After the templates have been fragmented, the barcodes used to tag fragments belonging to the same template are attached by overlap-extension PCR in the droplets (Fig. 2c). In this reaction, barcode sequences attach to the fragments through regions of sequence homology on the adaptor sequences added by the transposase.
The remaining droplets are chemically ruptured and the DNA contents are purified over a spin column, then size selected to remove free barcodes, resulting in a sequence-ready library.
Instances of multiple templates in the same barcode cluster are infrequent, and consistent with the rate of co-encapsulation expected by Poisson statistics (see Supplementary Note 3 for details).
However, bias in sequencing can yield excessive coverage in certain regions and insufficient coverage in others.
Droplet barcoding for massively parallel single-molecule deep sequencing
Lan, F. et al. Droplet barcoding for massively parallel single-molecule deep sequencing. Nat. Commun. 7:11784 doi: 10.1038/ncomms11784 (2016).

checks.rationale: The complete assigned SMDB row is represented by five connected transformations from DNA templates to pooled tagged DNA. The repeated droplets depict a compartment population on one route, with empty compartments retained; they do not denote separately named workflows or independent fractions requiring distinct operation instances. The only multi-input operation, barcoding, is a genuine joint reaction supported by the primary paper. Material identity, compartment persistence through barcoding, adaptor-bearing input history, and loss of compartments at the pooled endpoint agree across states, operations and edges. There are no depicted end-group structures or additional in-scope branches to preserve. Primary-supported mechanistic clarifications are distinguished from the poster, and no source conflict requiring a correction or consequential unresolved question was found.
